title: Anxiety's Body
hook: Anxiety is the body preparing for a danger that has not arrived, and from outside it is easily mistaken for rudeness, coldness or guilt.
why:
Anxiety is one of the most common experiences people have and one of the most misread. The new colleague who will not meet your eyes and answers in single words looks arrogant. The man at the party who stays by the wall gripping his drink looks unfriendly. The witness who fidgets and stumbles looks guilty. Each may be doing nothing more than coping with a body that is braced for a danger that is not there.

This chapter teaches what anxiety does to the body, how it shows from outside, why the things people do to manage it can make it worse, and how easily it is mistaken for something else. It also covers panic attacks, which are far more common than most people realise, and what to do when someone near you is having one. As in every chapter of this part, the aim is recognition and a kind response. Anxiety in its ordinary forms is part of being human; when it takes over someone's life, the right response is to help them reach treatment that works, not to diagnose it yourself.

teach.h: Anxiety is the alarm before the danger.
teach.p:
Psychologists often distinguish fear from anxiety. Fear is the response to a danger that is present: the car swerving towards you, the dog that lunges. Anxiety is the response to a danger that might come: the meeting tomorrow, the test results next week, the conversation that could go badly. The body's machinery is largely the same, the stress response described in the first chapter of this part, but in anxiety it runs ahead of events, sometimes for hours or days.

In small doses, anxiety is useful. It makes people prepare, check and take care. It becomes a problem when it is out of proportion to the real risk, when it lasts long after the risk has passed, or when it starts to shape a person's life around avoiding what they fear. Many people have an anxious temperament without ever having an anxiety disorder, and many people with severe anxiety hide it well.

For a reader, this has a clear consequence. When you see the signs of anxiety, you are seeing a body preparing for something. You do not know what, you do not know how serious it is, and you cannot tell from outside whether it is a passing worry, an anxious temperament or something that is taking over the person's life.

What you can usually tell is that the person's attention is partly elsewhere, on the danger they are anticipating, and that they are working harder than they appear to be just to be in the room with you.

An anxious person is often doing two things at once: talking to you, and watching for a threat you cannot see.
teach.disconfirm: If anxious people's bodies behaved no differently from calm people's, apart from what they reported feeling, anxiety would be invisible to a reader. The stress physiology described in this part makes that unlikely, though some people hide its outward signs very well.
teach.pullQuote: An anxious person is often doing two things at once: talking to you, and watching for a threat you cannot see.

teach.h: What anxiety looks like from outside.
teach.p:
Anxiety shows in most of the channels this book has described. The body tends to fidget: a knee bouncing, fingers tapping, a ring twisted, a pen clicked. Pacifiers increase, as the chapter on leakage and pacifiers described: hands to the neck, the face, the arms. Breathing quickens and rises, as the chapter on breath described, and the person may swallow often because the mouth goes dry. The voice tightens and may speed up or catch.

Gaze often changes. Some anxious people scan the room repeatedly, checking exits and faces. Many avoid eye contact, especially socially anxious people, for whom being looked at is the threat. Startle may be quicker: a dropped plate or a door slamming produces a bigger jump than it would in a calm person.

Some people go the other way. Instead of fidgeting, they freeze: very still, very quiet, answering in single words. Others become talkative, filling every silence to avoid the gaps where something might go wrong. Others become irritable, as the chapter on the I'm Fine mask described, which many men find easier to show than worry.

Anxiety also shows in behaviour over time: over-preparing, checking things several times, seeking reassurance, arriving very early, leaving very early, avoiding certain places or people.

None of these is specific to anxiety. Fidgeting can be boredom or ADHD; avoiding eye contact can be autism or culture; quietness can be introversion. As always, look for a change from baseline, a cluster, and a situation that might explain it.
teach.disconfirm: If fidgeting, gaze avoidance and quickened breathing were no more common in anxious moments than in calm ones, against a person's own baseline, they would tell you nothing about anxiety. Most people can observe the difference in themselves before a feared event.

teach.h: Safety behaviours keep the fear alive.
teach.p:
In 1995 David Clark and Adrian Wells described a model of social anxiety that has shaped its treatment ever since. A central idea is the safety behaviour: something an anxious person does in a feared situation to prevent the catastrophe they fear. Someone afraid of saying something stupid rehearses every sentence in their head before speaking. Someone afraid of being looked at avoids eye contact and stays at the edge of the room. Someone afraid their hands will shake grips a glass tightly or keeps them in their pockets.

The same year, Wells, Clark and colleagues described why these behaviours are a trap. They feel protective, but they stop the person from ever discovering that the feared catastrophe would not have happened anyway. The person leaves the party thinking *I got through it because I kept quiet*, not *people were friendly and nothing bad happened*. The fear survives intact for next time. Later treatment studies found that helping people drop their safety behaviours, while facing the situation, made treatment more effective.

Safety behaviours also change how anxious people look to others. Rehearsing sentences makes a person seem distracted. Avoiding eye contact makes them seem cold or evasive. Standing at the edge of the room makes them seem aloof. The very behaviours meant to prevent a bad impression often create one.

For a reader, recognising safety behaviours is a powerful correction. The man who seems uninterested in you may be working very hard to seem all right. And for yourself, if you carry anxiety, noticing your own safety behaviours is often the first step towards testing whether your fear is right.
teach.disconfirm: If dropping safety behaviours made no difference to how anxious people felt in feared situations, or made them worse over time, the model would be wrong. Treatment research built on the model found that dropping them helped.

teach.p:
Put the previous blocks together and you can see why anxiety is so often misread. The signs that anxious people show, and the behaviours they use to manage their anxiety, overlap almost exactly with the signs people associate with rudeness, coldness, arrogance, disinterest and guilt.

A job candidate who avoids eye contact, gives short answers and fidgets may be read as evasive, when she is terrified of interviews. A new colleague who eats alone and says little in meetings may be read as stuck-up, when he is rehearsing every sentence and finding none safe to say. A man questioned about a missing item who goes red, stumbles and touches his neck may be read as guilty, when he is anxious about being disbelieved, the Othello error described in the chapter on deception. A date who barely speaks may be read as uninterested, when she is overwhelmed.

The cost of these misreadings falls on people who are already struggling. Anxious people are often aware that they are coming across badly, which makes them more anxious, which makes them come across worse.

The correction is simple to state and harder to practise: when someone seems cold, rude or evasive, put anxiety on your list of rivals, early. Then respond in a way that would help if it were anxiety, and would do no harm if it were not: a little more warmth, a little more structure, a little less pressure. If the person is anxious, they will usually ease. If they are simply rude, you have lost nothing.

Before you decide someone is cold, consider that they may be frightened.
teach.disconfirm: If people you had read as cold or rude turned out, when you got to know them, rarely to have been anxious, the correction in this block would be unnecessary. Many people can think of someone they misjudged this way.

teach.h: Panic attacks are common, frightening and survivable.
teach.p:
A panic attack is a sudden surge of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within minutes, with strong bodily sensations: a pounding heart, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness, trembling, sweating, tingling, nausea, and often a terrifying sense that something catastrophic is happening, a heart attack, collapse, losing control or going mad. The chapter on breath described how over-breathing can feed the loop.

Panic attacks are far more common than most people think. In 2016 Peter de Jonge and colleagues analysed surveys of over 140,000 adults in twenty-five countries. About one adult in eight reported having had a panic attack at some point in their life. Most of them had had more than one. But only a small minority went on to meet the criteria for panic disorder, in which recurrent attacks and the fear of further attacks come to dominate a person's life.

From outside, a panic attack may look like a medical emergency, and sometimes people having one are taken to hospital for chest pain. It may also look like nothing much: some people have panic attacks quietly, sitting very still, gripping a chair, breathing hard, while those around them notice only that they have gone pale and silent.

For the person having one, the most important things to know are that panic attacks are not dangerous in themselves, that they pass, usually within minutes, and that they are very treatable. For the person beside them, the most important thing is the response in the next block.

A panic attack feels like dying. It is not, and it will pass.
teach.disconfirm: If panic attacks were rare, affecting only a tiny fraction of people, recognising them would matter less for most readers. The survey found about one adult in eight had experienced at least one, which makes it likely you will be near someone having one.

teach.h: Helping someone through a panic attack.
teach.p:
If someone near you seems to be having a panic attack, the first step is to check whether it might be something else. Ask whether they have chest pain, especially spreading to the arm or jaw, whether they have a heart or lung condition, asthma or diabetes, and whether this has happened before. If you are unsure, or if they do not improve, call the emergency services. Calling for a panic attack is a far smaller mistake than not calling for a heart attack.

If it does seem to be panic, stay with them. Move somewhere quieter if you can. Kneel or sit beside them rather than standing over them. Speak slowly and calmly, in short sentences: *I'm here. This is panic. It will pass. You're safe.*

Help them slow their breathing without making it a demand. Breathe slowly yourself where they can hear and see you, with a long breath out, and if they are open to it, invite them to breathe out with you. Paper bags are no longer recommended. Some people find it helps to focus on their senses: naming five things they can see, four they can hear, three they can touch, which draws attention away from the alarming sensations.

Avoid *calm down*, *it's all in your head* and *you're fine*. Each tells the person that their experience is wrong, which adds fear. Do not crowd them, and do not leave them alone unless they ask for space.

Afterwards, they may be exhausted, embarrassed or shaky. Be matter-of-fact and kind. If attacks keep happening, or they start avoiding places or activities because of them, encourage them to see a doctor. Talking therapies for panic and anxiety have good evidence and help most people.
teach.disconfirm: If staying calmly with someone, breathing slowly beside them and reassuring them it will pass made no difference to how quickly a panic attack subsided, the advice in this block would add nothing. Most people who have had panic attacks say that calm company helped.

teach.h: Give control and predictability, not endless reassurance.
teach.p:
Anxiety feeds on uncertainty and on the sense of having no control, which the first chapter of this part described in the research on stress. That points to what helps an anxious person day to day. Tell them what will happen and when. Send the agenda before the meeting. Say who will be at the dinner. Offer choices: where to sit, whether to speak first or last, whether to talk now or later. Predictability does not cure anxiety, but it removes some of what anxiety latches onto.

Reassurance is more complicated than it seems. When an anxious person asks *Are you sure it'll be all right?*, the natural response is *Yes, of course*. Clinicians who treat anxiety often find that repeated reassurance brings short relief and then the question comes back, sometimes within minutes, and that answering it over and over can help keep the worry going. A kinder response, after the first reassurance, is often to help the person make a plan, or to acknowledge the worry without arguing with it: *It sounds like this is really worrying you. What would help you feel ready?*

Gentle encouragement to face, not avoid, feared situations also helps, at a pace the person chooses. Avoidance shrinks a person's life and confirms the fear; small steps towards the feared thing, with support, are at the heart of most effective treatments.

And know when to suggest more. If anxiety is stopping someone from working, sleeping, travelling or seeing people, or if they are using drink to cope, encourage them to see a doctor. Effective help is widely available, and most people who get it improve.
teach.disconfirm: If repeated reassurance reliably reduced anxious people's worry for good, rather than briefly, the caution in this block would be unnecessary. Notice, the next time someone asks for reassurance repeatedly, how long the relief lasts.

poseGallery.doCaption: Wondering whether he is anxious, and making it a little easier.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Reading his avoided eyes and short answers as arrogance.
poseGallery.annotation: The signs of anxiety overlap almost exactly with those people read as rudeness or coldness. Put anxiety on your list of rivals early.

poseGallery.doCaption: Dropping one safety behaviour, and finding the fear was wrong.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Gripping a glass at the edge of the room, never testing the fear.
poseGallery.annotation: Safety behaviours feel protective but stop people discovering that what they fear would not happen. Dropping them, with support, helps.

poseGallery.doCaption: Kneeling beside him: 'I'm here. This will pass.'
poseGallery.annotation: Telling someone in a panic that they are fine tells them their experience is wrong. Calm company and slow breathing help more.

poseGallery.doCaption: Acknowledging the worry, and making a plan together.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Reassuring him for the tenth time that it'll be fine.
poseGallery.annotation: Repeated reassurance brings short relief and can keep worry going. A plan gives some control back.

poseGallery.doCaption: Brought into a small group, with something to do
poseGallery.dontCaption: Left alone at the edge of the party
poseGallery.annotation: An anxious guest holding his glass like a shield is not looking down on anyone. A role and one easy introduction lower the stakes.

poseGallery.doCaption: Settled, once he knows what comes next
poseGallery.dontCaption: A bouncing knee read as impatience
poseGallery.annotation: Restless legs often mean nerves, not boredom. Telling someone what will happen, and when, gives anxiety less to grip.

caseStudy:
Richard, fifty, leads a small finance team. His newest hire, Ollie, twenty-eight, is excellent on paper and quiet in person. In meetings he looks at the table, answers in a few words and never volunteers anything. He eats lunch alone at his desk. Two colleagues tell Richard they find Ollie stand-offish.

Richard watches more carefully. He notices that Ollie's knee bounces under the table in meetings, that he grips his pen tightly, and that his voice is tight and quick on the rare occasions he speaks. Before his first presentation to the department, Ollie arrives forty minutes early, and his hands shake as he sets up. None of it looks like arrogance. It looks like a man working very hard to get through each meeting.

Richard changes a few things without commenting on any of them. He sends agendas a day ahead, and tells Ollie in advance which item he will be asked about. He holds short one-to-ones before big meetings, so that Ollie can rehearse his points with one person rather than ten. He asks a warm, easy-going colleague to invite Ollie to the team's Thursday lunch.

After a month, in one of their one-to-ones, Ollie tells him that he has struggled with anxiety since university, that meetings are the hardest part of his job, and that the agendas have made a real difference. Richard thanks him for telling him, asks whether there is anything else that would help, and mentions the company's employee assistance programme. He does not tell anyone else.

In March Ollie presents to the department again. His hands still shake a little when he sets up. Afterwards, at lunch, he tells a joke.
observe: Notice one person this week who seems cold, rude or uninterested, and look for signs that they might instead be anxious.
Notice your own safety behaviours in a situation that makes you uneasy: what you do to prevent the thing you fear.
Notice how often someone asks for reassurance about the same worry, and how long the relief seems to last.

drills.name: Rivals for Rudeness
steps: Recall three people you have judged as cold, rude or arrogant on first meeting.
For each, write what they actually did, as behaviour.
Write how each behaviour could be explained by anxiety.
Note anything you later learned about any of them.
Write one thing you could do differently on a first meeting with someone who seems cold.
variations: Do the exercise for someone you judged as warm and confident on first meeting, and ask whether you missed any signs of nerves.
Ask a friend who describes themselves as shy how they think they come across to strangers, and compare it with how they do.

drills.name: Safety Behaviour Audit
steps: Choose a situation that makes you mildly anxious, such as a party, a phone call or speaking up in meetings.
List everything you do in that situation to prevent what you fear.
For each, write what you fear would happen without it.
Choose one behaviour to drop next time, in a low-stakes version of the situation.
Afterwards, write what actually happened.
variations: Ask someone you trust to watch you in a low-stakes version of the situation and tell you which safety behaviours they noticed.
Drop a different safety behaviour each time over a month, and keep a short record of what you feared and what happened.

drills.name: Panic Response Card
steps: Write down the questions you would ask to check for a physical emergency.
Write the emergency number where you live, and when you would call it.
Write three short, calm sentences you would say to someone having a panic attack.
Write the grounding exercise of naming things you can see, hear and touch.
Keep the card in your wallet or phone and read it once a month.
variations: Practise the card's sentences aloud with a friend playing the person having the attack, so that the words come easily.
Add to the card what you would say to bystanders, such as asking them to give space or to call for help.

drills.name: Predictability Offer
steps: Think of someone who seems anxious in a situation you share, such as a meeting or a family event.
Identify one piece of information you could give them in advance.
Identify one choice you could offer them.
Offer both, without mentioning anxiety.
Note any difference in how they seem.
variations: Try offering predictability to someone who seems confident, and notice whether it helps them too.
Offer a choice about the order of things, such as who speaks first, and notice whether the person takes it.

drills.name: Reassurance Swap
steps: Recall a time someone asked you repeatedly for reassurance about the same worry.
Write what you said each time.
Write an alternative response that acknowledges the worry without arguing with it.
Write a question that would help them make a plan.
Practise both aloud.
variations: Ask someone who gets anxious which responses help them most when they are worried, and add their answers to your notes.
Practise noticing the moment you are about to reassure for the second time, and swap in a question instead.

quiz.q: A new colleague avoids eye contact, gives short answers and eats lunch alone. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That he is arrogant and has decided he does not want to mix with you
That he is hiding something, and will be found out before long
That he may be anxious; make things a little easier and more predictable
That he has social anxiety disorder and should be told to get help
quiz.explain: These behaviours overlap closely with anxiety and safety behaviours. A little more warmth and structure helps if he is anxious and costs nothing if he is not. Diagnosing him, to his face or to others, is not your role.

quiz.q: In the World Mental Health Surveys analysed by de Jonge and colleagues, roughly what share of adults had ever had a panic attack?
options: About one in eight, most of whom had more than one
About one in a hundred, nearly all of them women
About half of all adults in every one of the countries
Almost nobody outside a small number of wealthy countries
quiz.explain: About one adult in eight reported at least one panic attack, and most had had several, but only a small minority developed panic disorder. You are likely to be near someone having one at some point.

quiz.q: According to the cognitive model of social anxiety, why do safety behaviours keep fear going?
options: They make the feared situation far more dangerous than it really is
They draw attention to the person, which then confirms the fear
They tire the person out so that they cannot cope with the situation itself
They stop the person discovering that the feared outcome would not happen
quiz.explain: Safety behaviours feel protective, but the person credits them with preventing a disaster that would not have happened. The fear survives intact, and dropping them, with support, helps treatment work.

quiz.q: A man in a café suddenly breathes very fast, grips the table and says he thinks he is dying. What fits this chapter?
options: Tell him firmly that it is only panic and that he will be absolutely fine in a minute
Check for chest pain or a known condition, stay calm beside him, breathe slowly
Give him a paper bag to breathe into until his breathing slows down again
Leave him to recover in peace, since crowding him will make it worse
quiz.explain: Check first for a physical emergency and call for help if unsure. If it is panic, calm company, slow breathing beside him and reassurance that it will pass help most. Paper bags are no longer advised.

quiz.q: Why can repeated reassurance backfire for an anxious person?
options: It makes the person angry with you for not taking them seriously
It tells the person that their worry is entirely justified and important
It brings short relief but can keep the worry coming back
It works so well that the person never learns to cope alone
quiz.explain: The relief fades and the question returns, sometimes within minutes. Acknowledging the worry and helping the person make a plan gives them some control, which tends to help more.

quiz.q: A friend has had several panic attacks this year and has started avoiding the supermarket where one happened. What fits this chapter?
options: Encourage him to see a doctor, since panic and anxiety respond well to treatment
Do his shopping for him from now on, so that he never has to go back there
Tell him to force himself to go every day until the fear goes away for good
Reassure him that panic attacks are harmless and that he should ignore them
quiz.explain: Recurrent attacks and growing avoidance are signs that help is worth seeking, and talking therapies have good evidence. Doing everything for him supports the avoidance; forcing him adds fear.

quiz.q: In Clark and Wells's model of social anxiety, where does an anxious person's attention often go in a feared situation?
options: Inward, to their own sensations and the impression they think they are making
Outward, to other people's faces, which anxious people read far more accurately than anyone else
Nowhere in particular, since anxiety has no effect on where people direct their attention
Towards the exits only, since anxious people are planning their escape the whole time
quiz.explain: Anxious people tend to turn their attention inward, to their racing heart and how they think they look. From outside this looks like disinterest, when it is the opposite.

quiz.q: A patient in a dentist's chair grips the armrests, breathes fast, keeps interrupting with questions and flinches at small movements. Staff call him rude. What fits this chapter best?
options: Ask him to stop interrupting so that you can get the treatment finished
Explain each step before you do it and agree a signal he can use to stop
Treat him exactly as you would any other patient, so as not to single him out
Tell him there is nothing to be afraid of and carry on as quickly as possible
quiz.explain: His cluster fits fear rather than rudeness. Anxiety eases with predictability and control, so explaining each step and agreeing a stop signal that works gives him both.

quiz.q: Someone says that the kindest way to help an anxious person is to arrange things so that they never have to face what frightens them. What does this chapter suggest?
options: It is right, since anxious people should be protected from every source of fear
This kind of accommodation can keep anxiety going; support small steps they choose
It is right for adults, though children should be pushed to face their fears at once
It is wrong, since anxious people should always be made to face their worst fears
quiz.explain: Accommodation comes from love but tends to maintain avoidance, and research on anxious children links it to more severe anxiety. Support the person, not the avoidance, with small steps they choose.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific person you misjudged as cold, rude, uninterested or evasive, and later suspected might have been anxious, or think of a time you were misjudged that way yourself. Describe what the body and behaviour actually showed. What safety behaviours, if any, can you now see in it? What would have helped in the first few minutes? And what is one situation in your own life where you could drop a safety behaviour this month?
reflection.guidance: Many men recognise themselves in this chapter, sometimes for the first time. Describing your own safety behaviours precisely is useful: they are often small and habitual, such as rehearsing sentences or keeping hands in pockets. The last question is the practical one. Choose a low-stakes situation, so that you can find out whether the fear is right.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to read anxiety as a character flaw, treating the anxious person as rude, cold, arrogant or guilty, and responding with coolness that makes them more anxious still. The second is the opposite: deciding that someone has an anxiety disorder and telling them or others so. The third is to respond to panic badly: telling someone to calm down, assuming panic when it may be a heart attack, or reaching for a paper bag. The fourth is to reassure endlessly, or to help someone avoid everything they fear, which keeps the anxiety going. And the most quiet failure is to miss your own anxiety and safety behaviours, which may be shaping your life more than you know. Warmth, structure, calm company, and encouragement towards treatment when it is needed, help most.

moreCases.title: The boyfriend by the wall
moreCases.scene:
Meg brings her new partner, Isaac, to her parents' fortieth wedding anniversary party. There are sixty people in a hired hall, most of them her relatives. Isaac shakes hands with her parents, says congratulations and then retreats to the wall beside the drinks table. For most of the next hour he stands there holding a glass of orange juice in both hands, close to his chest. He answers people who approach him politely but briefly, looks at the floor between sentences, and does not ask anyone a question. When Meg's uncle tries a joke, Isaac smiles tightly and says nothing.

Meg's brother, Rob, finds her in the kitchen. "What's his problem?" he asks. "He's acting like he's too good for us." Her aunt has said something similar.

Meg knows something Rob does not. Isaac told her before they arrived that big family events terrify him, that he had been awake half the night worrying about it, and that he would try his best. He had come anyway.

Meg also knows that Isaac is the funniest person she has ever met, one to one. He makes her laugh every day. Her family has seen none of that tonight, and she is starting to worry that they never will.

Isaac's position is also the same one he takes at every crowded event, Meg realises: with a wall behind him, near the drinks table, with a clear view of the door.
moreCases.misread:
Rob read Isaac's position by the wall, his short answers and his tight smile as arrogance, because those are the signs we expect from someone who looks down on the people around him. He did not consider that the same signs come from someone who is frightened of them.

And because Rob had decided Isaac was arrogant, he stopped trying to talk to him, which left Isaac more isolated and more anxious, and made him look more stand-offish still.

Rob also took Isaac's failure to ask questions as a lack of interest, when an anxious man's attention is often too busy watching himself to think of any.
moreCases.betterRead:
Anxiety and arrogance can look almost identical from outside: distance, short answers, little eye contact, a fixed position and a reluctance to join in. The difference is in what is going on inside, and that cannot be seen. Isaac's grip on his glass, held close like a shield, and his eyes dropping between sentences fitted anxiety far better than disdain, but even so, the kinder reading is the safer one to start with, because coldness towards an anxious person makes things worse. Meg's better approach was to give Isaac what anxiety needs: a little predictability and something to do. She asked him to help her carry round the plates of food, which gave him a role, a reason to move and a ready-made thing to say to each person. She introduced him to her cousin, who is also quiet and likes football, and left them by the window. By the end of the evening Isaac was laughing, and Rob admitted he had got him wrong.

Meg also told Isaac afterwards that he had done really well, and asked what had helped most. He said the plates, because they gave him something to hold that was not his own drink.

moreCases.title: The patient who seemed difficult
moreCases.scene:
Mr Kowalski, sixty, arrives at a dental surgery for a filling. At the desk he is curt, answering the receptionist's questions in a word. In the chair, he refuses to lie back fully. His hands grip both armrests so hard that his knuckles are white, his breathing is fast and high, and he keeps asking the dentist, Dr Shah, what she is about to do, interrupting her before she has finished explaining. When the nurse moves the light, he flinches. When Dr Shah picks up the drill, he sits bolt upright and says he needs a minute.

The receptionist has already told Dr Shah that Mr Kowalski is "rude". The nurse, who has a full list that afternoon, is visibly impatient.

Dr Shah notices that he has not been to a dentist for eleven years, according to his notes, and that he booked only after a tooth broke.

Mr Kowalski also mentions, as he sits down, that the last dentist he saw, as a young man, told him to stop being a baby and carried on when he asked her to stop.

He also keeps his coat on in the chair, zipped to the neck, and refuses the protective glasses at first, saying he wants to be able to see. When the nurse reclines the chair a few degrees, he grabs her wrist, then lets go and apologises, red in the face.
moreCases.misread:
The receptionist and the nurse read Mr Kowalski's curtness, gripping and interruptions as rudeness and awkwardness. They saw a difficult patient, when the signs fitted a frightened one.

The nurse's impatience also added to the threat. An anxious patient reads a hurried, irritated face as one more reason to be frightened.

They also assumed that a man of sixty who interrupts and grips is a man who wants to be in charge, when every one of his questions was a request for the predictability that his fear was demanding. His curtness at the desk was the first rung of the same fear.
moreCases.betterRead:
Fear of dental treatment is common, and it is one of the clearest examples of anxiety being misread as difficulty. The cluster was clear: a long gap since his last visit, curt answers, white knuckles, fast high breathing, constant questions and startle at small movements. Dr Shah's better reading led straight to what helps anxiety: predictability and control. She stopped, put the drill down and said, "A lot of people find this hard. Let's do it at your pace." She explained each step before she did it, and agreed a stop signal with him: if he raised his left hand, she would stop at once, no questions asked. He raised it twice during the filling, and both times she stopped, waited and went on when he nodded. His grip loosened as he found that the signal worked. At the end he apologised for being difficult. She told him he had not been difficult at all, and he booked a check-up for six months' time.

Dr Shah also wrote a note on his file, with his permission, about the stop signal, so that any dentist who saw him in future would know what helped.

moreCases.title: The student who stopped going to the hall
moreCases.scene:
Ana, nineteen, is in her first year at university, living in a hall of residence with a large shared dining hall. In the first week she ate there with her flatmates. By the fourth week she has stopped. She buys sandwiches and eats them in her room. When her flatmate Grace suggests dinner in the hall, Ana says she is not hungry, or has work to do. At seminars she sits by the door and does not speak unless asked a direct question, when her face goes red and her voice comes out very quietly. She has started missing the Thursday seminar altogether.

Grace, who likes Ana, has started to wonder whether Ana is avoiding her personally. Another flatmate thinks Ana is just antisocial and should be left alone.

One evening Grace finds Ana in the kitchen, late, eating cereal, and asks whether she is all right. Ana says she is fine, then adds, almost under her breath, that she cannot face walking into the hall with everyone looking at her.

Grace has also noticed that Ana texts her a lot, warmly and often, and is funny on the flat's group chat. In person, in a group, she is a different person: silent, pink-faced and watching the door.

Ana's mother rings most evenings, and Ana always says that university is great, that she is making lots of friends and that the food in the hall is lovely.
moreCases.misread:
Grace read Ana's withdrawal as being about her, and the other flatmate read it as a preference for being alone. Both readings missed the pattern that the withdrawal followed: away from the places where Ana felt watched.

And because Ana's withdrawal was quiet, it was easy to let it continue. Nobody notices when someone stops coming to dinner in a hall of three hundred people.

Grace's own worry, that it was about her, was also a form of self-focus, and a very common one. Most of us read other people's withdrawal as a verdict on ourselves.
moreCases.betterRead:
Clark and Wells described how people with social anxiety use safety behaviours, things they do to prevent the disaster they fear, and how avoidance is the most powerful of all. Each time Ana skipped the hall, she was spared the fear, and each time she lost the chance to find that people were not watching her as closely as she believed. The avoidance was spreading, from the hall to seminars. A friend cannot treat this, and should not try. What Grace could do was listen without judgment, tell Ana that she was far from the only person who felt like this, and offer practical company: walking into the hall together at a quiet time, sitting at a small table near the door. She also mentioned that the university's student support service had people who helped with exactly this, and offered to go with her. Ana went the following week, and started a course of therapy that worked on the fear directly. By the summer term she was eating in the hall most evenings.

Grace also kept inviting Ana to things, always with an easy way out.

moreCases.title: The young man in the supermarket queue
moreCases.scene:
Joan, fifty-four, is in the queue at a supermarket on a Saturday morning. The young man in front of her, in his early twenties, suddenly puts his basket down. He is breathing very fast, his hand is pressed to his chest and he is pale and sweating. He grips the edge of the conveyor belt and says, to nobody in particular, that he thinks he is going to pass out. People nearby step back. Someone mutters that he must be on something.

Joan used to work as a teaching assistant and has done a first aid course. She asks him his name, which is Harvey, and whether he has any pain in his chest or down his arm, any heart problems, asthma or diabetes. He says no, no pain, just his heart pounding, and that this has happened before, twice, and he thought he was dying both times.

The cashier asks whether she should call an ambulance.

Harvey's friend, who had gone to fetch something from another aisle, is nowhere to be seen. Harvey keeps looking towards the doors as if he wants to run, and his legs are shaking.

A security guard has started walking over, looking wary. Two teenagers further back in the queue are filming on their phones. Harvey sees them, and his breathing gets faster still.
moreCases.misread:
The people stepping back read Harvey's state as something to keep away from, and one of them read it as drug use. Both reactions left a frightened young man alone in public at the worst moment of his day.

The mutter about drugs also made Harvey's fear worse. Being judged by strangers is one of the things people fear most during a panic attack.

Nobody in the queue had done anything wrong exactly. They were frightened and uncertain, and stepping back is what frightened people do. But it left the most frightened person there alone.
moreCases.betterRead: Panic attacks are frightening and common, and they can look like many other things, including a medical emergency. Joan's first step was the right one: she checked for signs of a physical emergency before assuming panic. With no chest pain, no relevant conditions and a history of similar episodes, panic was the likely explanation, but she told the cashier to call an ambulance at once if anything changed or if he did not improve. She then did what helps: she moved him to a chair by the exit, away from the crowd, crouched beside him at his level, and spoke slowly and quietly. She told him that she thought it was a panic attack, that it would pass, and that she would stay with him. She did not tell him to calm down or to take deep breaths. She asked him to name five things he could see. Within about ten minutes his breathing had slowed and his colour had come back. She stayed until his friend arrived, and suggested gently that he mention the attacks to his doctor.

workedReading.title: The father at the school gate
workedReading.scene:
Funmi has been collecting her daughter from primary school for two terms. Most of the parents at the gate know each other and stand in small groups, chatting. One father, whom she knows only as Ethan's dad, always stands apart, by the railings at the far end, looking at his phone. If anyone approaches, he answers briefly and goes back to the phone. When the children come out, he leaves at once. Some of the other parents call him stand-offish. One says he is "a bit odd". This week, Ethan has invited Funmi's daughter to his birthday party, and she will have to speak to his father about it.

Funmi is not especially confident herself. She remembers standing alone at the gate in her first week, and how long the ten minutes felt before anyone spoke to her.

She has also heard what the other parents say, and she feels the small pull of agreeing with them. It would be easier to join in than to make up her own mind, and she notices that pull and puts it aside.

She also wonders how many of the parents who call him odd have ever said more than hello to him.

steps.label: Describe before judging
steps.text:
Funmi lists what she has actually seen. He stands apart, always in the same place. He looks at his phone rather than the people. He answers briefly when approached. He leaves quickly. She notes that the other parents have already turned these behaviours into a character, stand-offish and odd, and that she has not.

She also notices that every behaviour on her list puts distance between him and other people, and that none of them is aimed at anyone in particular. That is a pattern of avoidance, not of dislike.

She also writes down, in her head, what she has not seen: no rudeness to anyone, no complaint, no sign of contempt. A man who thought he was better than the other parents would probably show it in some way. He shows nothing at all.

steps.label: Look for the cluster
steps.text:
Next time she watches more closely, without staring. His shoulders are high. His thumb moves on the phone, but he does not seem to be reading anything. When a group nearby laughs, he glances up quickly and then down again. When the bell goes, he is already moving before the children appear. These look less like indifference than like a man waiting for an ordeal to end.

She also notes his arrival time. He arrives at the last possible moment, just before the bell, which keeps the waiting as short as it can be. That fits someone managing an ordeal.

She also notices that his phone screen is dark at least once while his thumb is still moving on it. The phone, she thinks, is less something to look at than somewhere to put his eyes.

steps.label: Hold the rival readings
steps.text:
He might be anxious in groups. He might be shy, or new to the area, or tired from night shifts, or simply a private man who does not like small talk. He might be going through something at home. Funmi notes that she cannot tell which, and that she does not need to. Whatever the reason, a big group approach would probably be unwelcome, and a small, easy one probably would not.

She also reminds herself that the kinder reading costs nothing if it is wrong. If he is simply private, a short, friendly question will not trouble him.

She also considers that he might simply not want to be approached, and decides that a short, practical question is the lightest way to test that. If he is curt, she will leave it there.

steps.label: Lower the demand
steps.text:
She chooses a moment when he is alone and nobody else is near, and approaches from the side rather than head on, so he can see her coming. She keeps it short and specific, with a reason to talk that is not about him: "Hi, I'm Amara's mum. Thanks for the party invitation. Is it all right if I drop her off and pick her up at the end?"

She also keeps her own body easy: hands visible, a small smile, standing a little to one side rather than square in front of him. A relaxed approach asks less of the person approached.

She also chooses a day when the gate is quiet, because it is raining and most parents are waiting in their cars.

steps.label: Give him predictability
steps.text:
He looks up, startled, then relaxes a little when he hears what she wants. He says yes, that is fine, and that it is at the soft-play place at two. She asks one more easy question, whether there is anything Amara should bring, and then says she will see him on Saturday. She leaves before the conversation can become a burden, which gives him a clean ending.

Leaving first also matters. An anxious person often does not know how to end a conversation, and fears getting it wrong. Ending it for him, warmly, removes one more thing to worry about.

She also gives him the information he will need without asking him to make small talk to get it: the time, the place, what to bring. Clear practical details are a gift to someone who dreads the unknown.

steps.label: Notice the change
steps.text:
At the party, he is still quiet, but he comes over when she arrives and tells her where the coats go. He says, with a small laugh, that he finds the school gate "a bit much" and that his wife usually does the pick-ups, but she started a new job in September. Funmi tells him she found it hard at first too, which is true.

She does not tell him that she had guessed he was anxious. He has told her something in his own words, and she lets him keep it that way.

She also tells him, briefly, that she is not great at the gate either. It gives him permission to have found it hard without making it a confession.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
Over the next few weeks, Funmi says hello to him at the gate each day, briefly, from the side, and sometimes stands near him for a minute or two. One day he walks over to her group, stands at the edge and joins in a conversation about the school play. The other parents start to say he is nice once you get to know him. Funmi notes that he was nice all along, and that what changed was how hard he had to work to show it.

She also notices that her daughter and Ethan have become close friends, and that Ethan's dad now waves at Amara by name. Small, predictable contact, repeated, did what one big conversation could not.

She also mentions to one of the other parents, lightly, that he is nice and just a bit shy, which changes the story the gate tells about him more than anything she could have said to him.

moreFailures.title: Reading anxiety as rudeness, coldness or guilt
moreFailures.body:
The safety behaviours that anxious people use, avoiding eye contact, keeping to the edges, answering briefly, leaving early, gripping something, are almost exactly the signs that others read as rudeness, arrogance, disinterest or guilt. The misreading has a cruel effect. People respond to perceived rudeness with coolness, and the anxious person, who was afraid of being judged, finds that they are being judged, which confirms the fear and deepens the anxiety. Before you decide that someone is cold, ask whether they might be frightened. If you are wrong, the warmth you offer will have cost you nothing.

It also helps to remember that anxious people often apologise afterwards for how they behaved, and that they remember the coolness they received long after you have forgotten it.

In workplaces, the misreading can cost people their jobs. An anxious new starter who is quiet in meetings and avoids small talk can be judged as not a team player within weeks, long before anyone has seen what they can do when they are settled.

moreFailures.title: Reassuring without end
moreFailures.body:
When someone is anxious, the natural response is to reassure them: it will be fine, you will be great, nothing bad will happen. Once, this can help. Repeated over and over, about the same worry, it tends to backfire. Each reassurance brings brief relief and teaches the person that they need it, so they ask again, and the worry is never tested. Reassurance can become a safety behaviour that someone else performs. A better response acknowledges the worry without arguing with it and helps make a plan: "I can see this is really worrying you. What would help you feel more ready?"

Reassurance can also be quietly undermining. Told repeatedly that there is nothing to worry about, an anxious person may conclude that their worry is foolish, which adds shame to the anxiety without removing either.

If someone asks for reassurance many times a day about the same thing, or cannot stop checking that something is safe, it may be worth gently suggesting that they talk to a doctor. Patterns like that can be part of anxiety conditions that respond well to treatment.

moreFailures.title: Pushing someone into the deep end
moreFailures.body:
Some people, having heard that avoidance keeps anxiety going, decide to help by forcing the anxious person to face what they fear: dragging a socially anxious friend to a party, putting a nervous colleague on the spot in a meeting, making a frightened child jump into the pool. This usually backfires. Facing fears does help, but it works best gradually, in steps the person chooses and controls, ideally with someone trained to guide it. Being pushed without consent tends to make the situation more frightening and the person less trusting. Offer company and small, optional steps. The choice is theirs.

With children especially, being forced can teach the opposite lesson: that the adults around them will not stop when they are frightened. That makes the next frightening thing harder, not easier.

It also helps to ask what the person themselves would like to try. Many anxious people have ideas about the steps they could manage, and are relieved to be asked rather than told.

And never use someone's anxiety as a joke or a test, by springing a surprise on them to see how they react. That teaches them that you are one more source of the unpredictability their anxiety fears.

moreFailures.title: Doing everything for them
moreFailures.body:
The opposite of pushing is accommodating: rearranging your life so that the anxious person never has to face what frightens them. You make every phone call, order every meal, answer the door, avoid the places they avoid. It comes from love, and it can keep the anxiety going. Research on families of anxious children, including work by Eli Lebowitz and colleagues, has found that this kind of accommodation is common and is linked to more severe anxiety over time, and that helping parents step back from it, supportively, can help children improve. The same principle applies to adults. Support the person, not the avoidance.

Stepping back does not mean withdrawing support. It means saying, warmly, "I know this is hard, and I'm sure you can do it," and letting them make the call, rather than making it for them.

Stepping back is easier when you tell the person what you are doing and why. "I'm not going to make the phone call for you this time, but I'll sit with you while you do" is support, not withdrawal.

It also helps to notice your own relief when you take over. If doing it for them feels easier for you, that is worth knowing, because it means the accommodation may be serving your anxiety as well as theirs.

questions.q: Can you tell anxiety from guilt by looking?
questions.a:
No. This is one of the most important lessons in the book, and the chapter on deception explains it in detail. An anxious honest person and a nervous liar show the same signs: fidgeting, avoided eyes, a dry mouth, a tight voice, a quick exit. Ekman called the mistake of reading an honest person's fear as guilt the Othello error. Anxiety under questioning is normal, especially in people who are anxious by temperament, who have been disbelieved before, or who are being questioned by someone with power over them. If you need to know whether someone is telling the truth, look at the evidence, not the body.

It also helps to remember that people who are questioned while anxious often give worse accounts, not better ones: they forget, hesitate and contradict themselves. None of that means they are lying.

It also helps to remember that some people look anxious all the time, by temperament, and that their anxiety tells you about them, not about whatever you are asking them.

And if you are the anxious one being questioned, it is reasonable to say so. "I get nervous in situations like this" often changes how the other person reads everything that follows.

questions.q: Why does anxiety make people seem cold?
questions.a:
Partly because of safety behaviours, and partly because of where an anxious person's attention goes. Clark and Wells described how, in feared social situations, anxious people turn their attention inward, to their racing heart, their hot face, the impression they think they are making, and away from the other person. From outside, that looks like disinterest: fewer questions, less warmth, less responsiveness. It is the opposite of disinterest. They care so much about how they are coming across that they have no attention left for the conversation itself. Making the situation more predictable and less evaluative frees some of that attention up.

It also explains why anxious people sometimes seem to ignore what you said. They heard it, but much of their attention was busy monitoring themselves. Repeating key information, or writing it down, can help.

The same inward focus also makes anxious people poor judges of how they came across. Many leave a conversation convinced they were awkward or boring, when the other person noticed nothing of the kind.

questions.q: Should I avoid situations that make someone anxious?
questions.a:
Not entirely, and not on their behalf without asking. Avoidance brings relief in the short term and tends to make anxiety worse in the long term, because the fear is never tested. But that does not mean pushing. A good middle path is to make situations easier rather than avoiding them: offer information in advance, a role to play, a quieter version, a way to leave if needed, company. Ask the person what would help, and let them choose how far to go. A friend's job is to make small steps possible, not to decide which steps they take.

It may also help to agree a way out in advance. Knowing that they can leave at any time, without explanation, often makes it easier for an anxious person to go in at all.

It also helps to check what you are avoiding on their behalf. Sometimes we steer an anxious friend away from things because we are anxious for them, not because they asked us to.

questions.q: What helps anxiety in the long run?
questions.a:
For anxiety that is persistent or getting in the way of life, there are effective treatments. Cognitive behavioural therapy, including approaches built on Clark and Wells's model of social anxiety, has a strong evidence base, and much of it works by helping people test their fears gradually and drop their safety behaviours. Medication can also help some people. Many people with anxiety never seek treatment, often because they are anxious about seeking it. A friend can help by making it ordinary to talk about, and by helping with the practical steps of getting an appointment.

Self-help books based on the same approach, such as the one listed in this chapter's further study, can also help people with milder anxiety, especially as a first step or while they wait for an appointment.

It also helps to know that treatment works best when it is started, not when it is perfect. A first appointment, even an awkward one, is a step that many anxious people take only because someone made it feel ordinary.

questions.q: What should I say to someone who is anxious before something big?
questions.a:
Avoid "don't worry" and "you'll be fine", which tend to feel dismissive and invite the person to explain why they will not be. Instead, acknowledge the feeling and offer something concrete. "It makes sense you're nervous, it's a big day." "What's the bit you're most worried about?" "Would it help to run through it once?" "I'll be in the second row if you want a friendly face." Information about what will happen, a plan for the hardest moment, and company all help more than predictions that everything will be all right.

It also helps to say what you will do, not only what they will feel. "I'll text you when I'm outside" is more calming than "You'll be fine", because it is something they can count on.

It can also help to share your own experience lightly: "I always feel sick before I present." Hearing that nerves are normal, from someone who copes, can make them feel less like a sign of failure.

questions.q: How do I know when it is more than ordinary nerves?
questions.a:
You cannot diagnose anxiety in someone else, but you can notice when it seems to be costing them a great deal. Signs worth taking seriously include anxiety that lasts for months, that stops someone doing things they want or need to do, that leads them to avoid more and more places or people, that comes with repeated panic attacks, or that seems to be affecting their sleep, work or relationships. In those cases, it is worth asking gently whether they have thought about talking to a doctor, and offering to help. If someone's anxiety comes with hopelessness or thoughts of not wanting to be here, 2.13 describes what to do.

It also helps to know that anxiety and low mood often go together, and that a person who has been very anxious for a long time may also be worn down. Asking about sleep, energy and enjoyment can help you understand how they are.

It also helps to know that many people with anxiety describe it as physical first: stomach trouble, headaches, a tight chest, poor sleep. Those may be the easiest things to talk about, and the easiest to take to a doctor.

watch.title: What causes panic attacks, and how can you prevent them?
watch.notice: An animated lesson on panic attacks. Notice the physical symptoms it describes, and how easily they can be mistaken for something else, by the person having them as well as by those around him.

reviewPrompt: The next time someone seems cold or rude, put anxiety on your list of rivals, and offer a little more warmth and structure before deciding.
